subject: psychology
title: Approaches: Behaviourism & Cognitive
welcome_lead: From Pavlov's dogs to the mind as a computer — two cornerstones of psychology.
meta_desc: A-Level Psychology approaches: behaviourism Pavlov Skinner, cognitive information processing.
final_note: Behaviourism studies the observable; cognitive psychology infers the unseen.

concepts.def: Adding a reward to increase behaviour frequency.
Removing an aversive to increase behaviour frequency.
Mental framework of organised knowledge guiding processing.
Mapping cognition onto brain — emerged in the 1970s.

walkthroughs.body_html: Pavlov (1902) paired a bell (NS) with food (UCS). After repeats the bell alone (CS) made dogs salivate (CR). Skinner (1953) built a box where rats learned to press a lever for food (positive reinforcement) or to stop a shock (negative reinforcement). Punishment reduces behaviour.

The cognitive approach treats the mind as analogous to a computer: input, encode, store, retrieve, output. It infers mental processes from behaviour using models like the MSM. Schemas (Bartlett 1932) explain how prior knowledge biases new information.

From the 1970s, fMRI and PET let researchers map cognition. Tulving (1989) showed episodic and semantic memory activate different prefrontal areas. Broca's area (1861) was an early case of cognition being localised. Today's neuroscience extends behaviourist and cognitive ideas with biology.
